{"id": "24:27/q06", "question": "Was tastaʾnisū also read as tastaʾdhinū, and how are the scribal-error reports assessed?", "turns_on": "Whether the reported alternative is a Qurʾānic reading, a gloss, a choice among aḥruf, or an unreliable scribal-error attribution in light of the agreed codices.", "positions": [{"id": "24:27/q06/p1", "position": "Some reports give tastaʾdhinū, 'ask permission,' sometimes attributing it to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ubayy, al-Aʿmash or ʿAbd Allāh and claiming a scribe erred.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr are cited for the error report; some transmissions also give greeting first. Al-Ālūsī says the report has many routes and cites al-Ḍiyāʾ's Mukhtāra, praised by al-Sakhāwī, al-Suyūṭī and Ibn Rajab. Al-Ṭabrisī, al-Durr, al-Itqān and others preserve variants. Ibn Ashtah's reconciliation treats the error as choice among seven aḥruf, though al-Ālūsī says this strains Ibn ʿAbbās's words and the Companions' agreement."}, {"id": "24:27/q06/p2", "position": "The received tastaʾnisū is sound Arabic and agreed in the codices; tastaʾdhinū may be an explanatory gloss, and the error attribution is rejected or weakened.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says a grave error could not have been universally accepted. Al-Zamakhsharī deems the report unreliable. Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites the agreed ʿUthmānic codices, the weakness of the other reading and Ibn ʿAbbās's own gloss; al-Rāzī adds mass transmission. Qurtubi cites 41:42 and 15:9 and Companion consensus. Abū Ḥayyān calls the attribution heretical. Al-Samīn calls it fabricated. Ibn al-Anbārī weakens conflicting reports; al-Ālūsī finds Ibn Ashtah's harmonization strained. Abū Ḥayyān states the received word is meaningful Arabic."}]}
{"id": "24:27/q07", "question": "Does the morphology of istiʾnās allow derivation from ānasa?", "turns_on": "Whether the morphological relation between afʿala and istifʿala supports this lexical derivation.", "positions": [{"id": "24:27/q07/p1", "position": "The verb's morphology prevents deriving it from ānasa.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya states this objection; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn transmit it."}, {"id": "24:27/q07/p2", "position": "The istifʿala form can be connected with sensing or seeking what makes visitor and household at ease.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya describes ānasa as afʿala and istaʾnasa as istifʿala; al-Zajjāj and other lexical explainers use the knowing/perceiving sense and 4:6."}]}
{"id": "24:27/q08", "question": "In what order should one announce, greet and request permission?", "turns_on": "Whether recited order governs action, whether the wording is transposed, whether seeing occupants changes the sequence, and whether wāw imposes any chronology.", "positions": [{"id": "24:27/q08/p1", "position": "Greet first, then ask permission; the verse's wording puts the acts in a different order from their performance.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā, al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī and al-Wāḥidī cite the fronting and delay; Ibn Masʿūd's codex puts greeting first. Al-Wāḥidī compares ordered pairs in 3:43 and 64:2. Ibn ʿUmar, ʿĀʾisha, the Rawḍa visitor and Kaldah reports demonstrate greeting followed by request. Al-Nawawī prefers greeting first based on reports that it precedes speech and an ungreeted requester is not admitted. Rāzī rejects transposition as weaker than the apparent wording; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects it. Al-Māwardī also reports greeting first as the legal order. Al-Ṭabrisī reports this parsing. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī transmits the Rawḍa instruction."}, {"id": "24:27/q08/p2", "position": "Seek notice or permission first, then greet, following the verse's stated order.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports greeting after permission. Al-Baghawī reports a group saying 'May I enter? Peace be upon you.' Rāzī says a visitor may first need to know whether anyone is present, then greet face to face; al-Qurṭubī takes Abū Ayyūb's announcement report as confirmation. Ibn Kathīr describes divine manners in this order. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī takes signaling before greeting."}, {"id": "24:27/q08/p3", "position": "The sequence depends on whether the occupants are seen: greet first if seen, otherwise ask permission first.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī, al-Nasafī and al-Māwardī report the distinction; al-Qurṭubī says eye contact obliges greeting but does not itself grant entry."}, {"id": "24:27/q08/p4", "position": "Both acts are required without an obligatory order; greeting first is preferable according to reports.", "reasons": "Rāzī and Ibn ʿĀshūr say coordinating wāw does not set chronology. Ibn ʿĀshūr says either order meets the conjunctive command; Kuran Yolu quotes Nawawī that the recited order need not be followed."}]}
{"id": "24:27/q09", "question": "What counts as a request for entry, and what must the visitor say or do?", "turns_on": "Whether the visitor must use the reported formula or any clear, courteous means of requesting entry.", "positions": [{"id": "24:27/q09/p1", "position": "A clear greeting and request such as 'Peace be upon you; may I enter?' is the proper formula; identify oneself, and use a gentle signal if needed.", "reasons": "Reports of the Prophet correcting the blunt visitor and Kaldah establish the formula. Ibn ʿUmar, ʿĀʾisha and Abū Hurayra withhold entry until greeting and explicit invitation. Saying only 'I' fails to identify a caller, as the Jābir incident and later anecdotes illustrate. Al-Māwardī permits verbal, gestural or loud requests; Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Qurṭubī allow customary wording, illustrated by Persian andar. Rāzī bars pounding and shouting, citing 49:4; Qurṭubī recommends soft knocking, mentions fingernails and reports garden-well knocking. Kuran Yolu applies clear identification to bells and intercoms."}, {"id": "24:27/q09/p2", "position": "The wording is flexible: gesture, announcement, knocking, customary speech or an appropriate signal can convey a request or alert the household.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī counts a gesture or loud call. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Qurtubi allow local phrases; Ibn ʿĀshūr denies a fixed formula. Ibn Kathīr, al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī mention sounds. Al-Ālūsī says they must convey a request and notice. Al-Qurṭubī's Persian expression and Abū Hurayra incident show non-Arabic usage."}]}
{"id": "24:27/q10", "question": "How many times may entry be requested without an answer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "24:27/q10/p1", "position": "Ask or greet up to three times, spaced to allow hearing and preparation; leave after the third unanswered or refused request.", "reasons": "The Abū Mūsā and ʿUmar report has corroboration by Ṭalḥa or Abū Saʿīd, with ʿUmar seeking proof rather than suspecting him. Qatāda assigns hearing, preparation and decision to the three requests; al-Ḥasan says permission, consultation and final notice. Rāzī and Elmalılı require intervals; Qurtubi says three usually ensure comprehension and that insistence burdens hosts, citing Saʿd's quiet replies to obtain more greetings. Malik permits another request if certain the first was unheard; Abū Ḥayyān and Kuran Yolu give the same exception. Ibn Kathīr calls the Saʿd report good despite uncertain attribution to Anas and another route. Al-Bayḍāwī also cites the three-request Prophetic rule."}]}
{"id": "24:27/q11", "question": "Does seeking permission alone permit entry, and what can count as consent?", "turns_on": "Whether the assent has already been conveyed by an invitation, authorized person or standing custom.", "positions": [{"id": "24:27/q11/p1", "position": "Entry requires an actual invitation or permission, whether explicit or conveyed by an authorized messenger or invitation.", "reasons": "Rāzī argues the purpose is not met by a bare request and 24:28 requires permission when nobody is found; reports from Abū Hurayra make an invitation-bearing messenger sufficient. Ibn ʿUmar presses a woman to say plainly 'enter,' since 'enter in peace' may invite only greeting. Rāzī says even a child, woman, slave or non-Muslim can convey permission, since this is not testimony. Kuran Yolu extends prior invitation to a specified time and place and recognizes public authorization. Elmalılı calls unauthorized entry into a house where one has no right an assault."}, {"id": "24:27/q11/p2", "position": "A person customarily allowed to enter may not need a fresh request.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports this juristic qualification without adopting it."}]}
{"id": "24:27/q12", "question": "Whose rooms require permission, including family and one's own home?", "turns_on": "Whether the space is privately occupied, whether close kinship removes a duty to ask, and whether announcement suffices where one already has a right to enter.", "positions": [{"id": "24:27/q12/p1", "position": "Permission is required before entering relatives' private spaces, including mothers' and sisters' rooms, even in a shared home.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAṭāʾ, Mālik and others require it. Qurtubi recommends an audible warning; Elmalılı treats a room occupied by someone else as private even inside one's own property. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī transmits the mother's nakedness report. Abū Ḥayyān transmits the same exchange."}, {"id": "24:27/q12/p2", "position": "Entry to one's own home with wife or family needs no formal permission, though greeting or announcing oneself is recommended.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ exempts one's wife; Ibn Kathīr says this denies obligation only and recommends warning her. Qurtubi says greet family and cites Qatāda; Aḥmad recommends throat-clearing or moving sandals, and Ibn Kathīr cites reports against surprising family at night. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the dwelling with wife or slave woman one's own. Rāzī exempts wives and owned slave women if the reason is avoiding exposure of nakedness; he says interruption of private activity would require warning even them. Abū Ḥayyān takes th

{"id": "24:27/q13", "question": "What is required before entering an unoccupied or public house?", "turns_on": "Whether the house is public, privately owned and empty, or one's own; and whether the later verse exempts or abrogates the first.", "positions": [{"id": "24:27/q13/p1", "position": "Unoccupied public places open for use are excepted from separate permission by 24:29.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās calls the later verse an abrogation or exception; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects abrogation, distinguishing inhabited and public uninhabited houses. Kuran Yolu lists inns, hotels, washrooms, shops and abandoned buildings with stored fuel, explaining 'belongings' also as places made available for use. Al-Zajjāj and Rāzī cite the next verse's consent condition."}, {"id": "24:27/q13/p3", "position": "When entering one's own empty home, utter a blessing for oneself and God's righteous servants; another view omits greeting and permission.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima and Qatāda give blessing formulas; Qatāda says angels answer. {"id": "24:27/q14", "question": "May someone peer through a doorway or window before permission, and how should the visitor stand?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "24:27/q14/p1", "position": "Looking in before permission is prohibited or counts as entry; stand to the side of an open doorway and protect the household's privacy.", "reasons": "The Prophet's reports to Sahl, Saʿd and Abū Saʿīd say permission was instituted because of sight; homes then lacked curtains. {"id": "24:27/q15", "question": "Is there compensation if a householder blinds an unauthorized peeper?", "turns_on": "Whether the eye-forfeit reports state an operative exception, a case of resisted persistence, or figurative warning in light of general injury rules.", "positions": [{"id": "24:27/q15/p1", "position": "The peeper's eye is forfeit, so the householder owes neither compensation nor retaliation.", "reasons": "Al-Shāfiʿī rules this way; Abū Hurayra's and other Prophetic reports state it. {"id": "24:27/q20", "question": "In what sense is this practice 'better for you'?", "turns_on": "Whether 'better' compares with abrupt entry and old greetings or simply states goodness.", "positions": [{"id": "24:27/q20/p1", "position": "Permission and greeting are better than sudden entry or pre-Islamic greetings because they protect privacy, avoid sin and suspicion, let residents prepare, and benefit both sides.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr compare uninvited entry; al-Naḥḥās says it creates suspicion.
